notes: Community pack continuing the series after Neighbourhood, Safety & Civic Voice. 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

tracks.name: Devices, accounts and the keys you hold

themes.theme: What a device knows about you
themes.description: The sensors, logs and identifiers a phone or laptop carries, and which of them keep working when the screen is off.
themes.transfer_check: Open the settings of a real device and list three things it records that you did not switch on.

bands.K–2: Name one thing a tablet remembers, with an adult looking at settings together.
bands.3–5: Find two things a family device remembers about its use, with an adult.
bands.6–8: List three sensors or logs on a real device that work even with the screen off, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Audit a real device's sensors and logs and say which keep working with the screen off.
bands.11–12: Explain to a younger user, with evidence from settings, what a device tracks and why it matters.

themes.theme: An account is a key, not a place
themes.description: What an account actually is, what the provider holds, and what you lose the day it is closed or locked.
themes.transfer_check: Pick one account you rely on and write down what would be lost if it vanished tonight, then export or copy the one thing that matters most.

bands.K–2: Say what a login and password are for, with an adult's help.
bands.3–5: Explain why a shared family account still needs its own password for you.
bands.6–8: Explain what a provider can see or do with your account, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real account you use, exactly what the provider holds and controls.
bands.11–12: Teach someone new to a service what an account actually is and is not, in their own words.

themes.theme: Passwords, passkeys and the second factor
themes.description: Why one strong secret per account beats one clever secret everywhere, and what a second factor actually defends against.
themes.transfer_check: Turn on a second factor for a real account and explain what attack it just blocked.

bands.K–2: Help an adult pick a strong password by making it long and silly together.
bands.3–5: Make up one long, strong password of your own for a practice account.
bands.6–8: Set up a second factor on a real account, with a checker confirming it works.
bands.9–10: Set up passkeys or a second factor on every real account that offers one.
bands.11–12: Explain to a household why one strong secret per account beats reusing one clever one.

themes.theme: Recovery: proving you are you
themes.description: Recovery emails, codes and trusted contacts — the quiet path attackers love and owners forget.
themes.transfer_check: Run the account-recovery path for one of your accounts before you need it and record where it broke or held.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult which grown-up should be able to help you get back into an account.
bands.3–5: Write down a trusted adult's name as your account's recovery contact.
bands.6–8: Set a real recovery email or code for one of your own accounts, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Configure recovery methods on your own real accounts without help.
bands.11–12: Set up and explain a family's recovery plan across several real accounts.

themes.theme: The shared device
themes.description: Profiles, guest modes and what a borrowed or family device remembers of the person who used it.
themes.transfer_check: Set up a shared device so two people can use it without reading each other's messages, and demonstrate it.

bands.K–2: Find your own profile picture on a shared family tablet, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Switch to your own profile on a shared device without mixing up files.
bands.6–8: Set up a guest mode on a shared device correctly, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Configure a shared device's profiles so no one sees another's files by accident.
bands.11–12: Set up a household's shared devices with profiles and guest modes for every member.

themes.theme: Updates, backups and the boring habits
themes.description: What an update actually patches, what a backup actually restores, and the schedule that makes both invisible.
themes.transfer_check: Restore one real file from a backup you made yourself.

bands.K–2: Watch an adult install an update and ask what it changed.
bands.3–5: Remind an adult when a device says it needs an update.
bands.6–8: Run a real update and a real backup on a device, with a checker confirming both worked.
bands.9–10: Keep a real device updated and backed up on your own schedule.
bands.11–12: Set up automatic updates and backups for a household's devices and explain why each matters.

themes.theme: When a device is lost or taken
themes.description: Remote lock, remote wipe and the order of phone calls in the first hour after a device disappears.
themes.transfer_check: Write the first-hour checklist for your own device, with the real account names, and test that you can trigger the lock.

bands.K–2: Practice saying who to tell first if a family tablet goes missing, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Name the first three calls to make if a device is lost, with an adult checking.
bands.6–8: Use a real device's remote lock feature in a practice run, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Remote-lock or wipe a real lost device and make the right calls in the right order.
bands.11–12: Write a lost-device plan for a household and walk someone else through it.

themes.theme: Scams that arrive as messages
themes.description: Phishing, smishing and the urgent-parcel text: the shapes these take and the two checks that defeat most of them.
themes.transfer_check: Take a real suspicious message you or your family received and show, step by step, how you decided what it was.

bands.K–2: Point out one thing that looks wrong in a fake message an adult shows you.
bands.3–5: Spot two warning signs in a practice phishing text with an adult.
bands.6–8: Correctly identify a real phishing or smishing attempt, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Correctly identify and report a real scam message without help.
bands.11–12: Teach a family member the shapes scam messages take, using real examples you've seen.

themes.theme: Permissions: what an app may touch
themes.description: Camera, contacts, location, files — reading an app's permissions as a list of things it can do without asking again.
themes.transfer_check: Audit the permissions of three installed apps and revoke one grant that the app does not need to do its job.

bands.K–2: Point at the camera or microphone icon when an app asks to use it, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Say no to one app permission that seems unnecessary, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Review a real app's permission list and turn off one unneeded one, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Audit every app on your own device and correct unneeded permissions.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how to read an app's permission request before granting it.

themes.theme: The account after a life change
themes.description: Moving out, breaking up, leaving a job, a death in the family — the accounts that must change hands or be closed, and how.
themes.transfer_check: For one real or rehearsed life change, list the accounts affected and complete the handover or closure steps for one of them.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens to an account when someone moves house.
bands.3–5: List two accounts that would need updating if your family moved, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Update one real account's details after a real change, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Handle your own account changes after a real move, job or relationship change.
bands.11–12: Guide a family member through updating their accounts after a major life change.

tracks.name: Information: what to trust and how to check

themes.theme: Where a claim was born
themes.description: Tracing a screenshot, quote or statistic back to the first place it appeared, and what changes along the way.
themes.transfer_check: Take one claim from today's feed and trace it to its original source, noting each hop.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult where a surprising claim in a video first came from.
bands.3–5: Trace a simple claim back to the first place it was posted, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Trace a real screenshot or quote back to its original source, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace a real viral claim back to where it was first posted, on your own.
bands.11–12: Show someone else, step by step, how you traced a real claim back to its origin.

themes.theme: Who is speaking and who is paying
themes.description: Bylines, about pages, sponsors and the difference between a newsroom, a marketer and a stranger with a logo.
themes.transfer_check: For one article you read this week, identify the author, the publisher and the likeliest source of money, with evidence.

bands.K–2: Point out the name of who made a video, with an adult's help.
bands.3–5: Find the 'about' page of a website and say who runs it, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify who is speaking and who paid for a real piece of content, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify sponsorship or bias in a real byline or about page on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the difference between a reporter, an advertiser and a sponsor.

themes.theme: The picture that proves too much
themes.description: Old photos in new stories, crops that change meaning, and generated images — the checks that take under two minutes.
themes.transfer_check: Run a reverse-image search on a real image from your feed and report what it was originally.

bands.K–2: Notice when a photo an adult shows you looks old or out of place.
bands.3–5: Spot one clue that a photo might be from a different event, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Check a real photo's origin using a reverse image search, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Verify a real photo's date and context on your own before believing it.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else to check a suspicious photo's origin and context.

themes.theme: Numbers that feel true
themes.description: Percentages without denominators, axes that start at nine hundred, and averages that hide the person in front of you.
themes.transfer_check: Find one misleading number or chart in the wild and rewrite it so it says the honest version.

bands.K–2: Notice when a chart an adult shows you looks stretched or squished.
bands.3–5: Spot a chart axis that doesn't start at zero, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Find the missing denominator in a real percentage claim, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Catch a real misleading statistic and explain what's missing, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why a real number 'feels true' but is actually misleading.

themes.theme: The feed is an argument
themes.description: Ranking, recommendation and why two people searching the same words see different worlds.
themes.transfer_check: Compare the same search or topic across two accounts or devices and document three differences in what was shown.

bands.K–2: Notice that your tablet shows different things than an adult's, with their help.
bands.3–5: Compare what you and a family member see in the same app, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain why two real searches on the same term differ, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real feed, how ranking shapes what you see and why.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how a real recommendation feed is built to keep them there.

themes.theme: Headlines and the gap before the click
themes.description: What a headline is for, what it leaves out, and the habit of reading before sharing.
themes.transfer_check: Take three headlines, predict the substance of each story, then read them and score your predictions.

bands.K–2: Guess what a headline an adult reads aloud might be hiding.
bands.3–5: Read a real headline and guess what it leaves out, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Compare a real headline to its article and name what's missing, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read past a real headline before forming an opinion, on your own, every time.
bands.11–12: Show someone else how a real headline was written to get a click, not to inform.

themes.theme: Checking without an expert
themes.description: Lateral reading: leaving the page to see what others say about the source before believing the source about itself.
themes.transfer_check: Fact-check one unfamiliar site by lateral reading and deliver a verdict with two independent confirmations.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult to open another tab to check a claim together.
bands.3–5: Open a second website to check a claim, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Use lateral reading to check a real claim across other sources, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Fact-check a real claim using lateral reading on your own, without an expert.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else the lateral-reading method using a real claim you checked.

themes.theme: When the truth is genuinely unsettled
themes.description: Live events, early science and rumours in a crisis — holding a question open without falling for the first confident answer.
themes.transfer_check: Pick one unsettled question in the news and write what is known, what is claimed, and what would settle it.

bands.K–2: Say 'we don't know yet' about a fast-changing story, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Notice that a breaking-news story keeps changing, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Track how a real unfolding story's facts changed over a week, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Hold uncertainty about a real unsettled event without repeating early rumours.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why early reports on a real crisis are often wrong, and why.

themes.theme: Your own share button
themes.description: What resharing asserts, who inherits the correction when you are wrong, and the repair that actually works.
themes.transfer_check: Write and, where real, post the correction for something you or someone near you shared that turned out false.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult before sharing something you saw online.
bands.3–5: Explain to an adult why you want to share something before you do it.
bands.6–8: Decide whether to share a real post and explain your reasoning, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Decide, on your own, whether a real post is worth resharing and correct it if needed.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what resharing asserts and who owns the correction afterward.

themes.theme: Archives, receipts and what persists
themes.description: Screenshots, archive links and edit histories — keeping evidence of what was said when it matters later.
themes.transfer_check: Capture one page with an archive service and explain when the archive, not the live page, is the record you want.

bands.K–2: Take a screenshot with an adult's help to save something important.
bands.3–5: Save a screenshot of something that might disappear, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Use an archive link to save a real page before it changes, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Archive a real page or edit history on your own before it disappears.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to keep a durable record of a real online claim.

tracks.name: Privacy and the trail you leave

themes.theme: The trail you cannot see
themes.description: Location history, search history, purchase records — the logs that accumulate by default and who can read them.
themes.transfer_check: Download or view one of your own data histories and name two things in it you did not expect.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a map app remembers about where you've been.
bands.3–5: Name one thing an app records about you without you seeing it, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find your own real location history or search history, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Review and clear your own real location or search history on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what a trail of invisible data looks like, using a real example.

themes.theme: What 'free' is paid with
themes.description: Advertising, profiling and the trade behind a free service, read from the privacy policy's first honest paragraph.
themes.transfer_check: For one free service you use, state in two sentences what it collects and how it earns, citing its own policy.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult why a free game keeps showing ads while you play.
bands.3–5: Explain that a free app makes money some other way, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Identify what a real free service is paid with, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real free service you use, exactly what you trade for it.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else the business model behind a real 'free' product.

themes.theme: Settings that actually matter
themes.description: The five privacy switches worth finding on any service, and the many that are decoration.
themes.transfer_check: Change three privacy settings on a real account and explain what each now prevents.

bands.K–2: Find one privacy setting on a family device with an adult.
bands.3–5: Turn on one privacy setting on a practice account, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find and adjust two of the five privacy switches that matter on a real service, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Adjust all five key privacy settings on your own real accounts.
bands.11–12: Write a short guide to the five privacy settings worth finding on any service.

themes.theme: Other people's data in your hands
themes.description: The photo with someone else in it, the contact list you upload, the group chat you screenshot — being trustworthy with data about others.
themes.transfer_check: Before sharing one real photo or screenshot involving another person, run a consent check and record the outcome.

bands.K–2: Ask a friend before posting a photo with them in it, with an adult watching.
bands.3–5: Ask permission before sharing a photo of a friend, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Get real consent before posting a real photo or contact list, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Handle other people's data responsibly in a real situation, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why the photo or contact list they hold belongs partly to others too.

themes.theme: Children, elders and the ones you manage
themes.description: Accounts you run for someone else: what protection looks like without surveillance, at every age.
themes.transfer_check: For one account you manage for another person, write the rules you follow and review them with that person at their level.

bands.K–2: Help a younger sibling pick a safe picture for their profile, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Help set up a safe account for a younger sibling, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Set up and manage a real account for someone younger or older who needs help, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Manage a real account for a dependent, on your own, protecting their data properly.
bands.11–12: Advise a family on setting up safe accounts for children or elders in their care.

themes.theme: What an employer or school may see
themes.description: Managed devices, monitored networks and the difference between your account and their account with your name on it.
themes.transfer_check: List which of your daily tools are managed by an institution and what each can log, then move one personal habit off them.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what a school computer can see that you do.
bands.3–5: Name one thing a monitored school network might track, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify what a real managed device or monitored network actually sees, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Distinguish, for a real managed device, what is monitored from what is private.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real difference between a personal and a managed device.

themes.theme: Data breaches and what to do after
themes.description: Breach notices, credential stuffing and the reset-and-rotate routine that limits the damage.
themes.transfer_check: Check a real email address against a breach-notification service and complete the follow-up for anything found.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what to do if a service says your information leaked.
bands.3–5: Explain why you'd need a new password after a leak, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Respond correctly to a real breach notice by resetting a password, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Handle a real breach notice on your own — reset, rotate, and check for reuse.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else the reset-and-rotate response to a real data breach.

themes.theme: Asking for your data back
themes.description: Access, export and deletion requests — the rights that exist where you live and the buttons that exercise them.
themes.transfer_check: Submit one real export or deletion request and report what came back and how long it took.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult what happens when you ask a company to delete something.
bands.3–5: Ask an adult to help you find a company's 'delete my data' option.
bands.6–8: Submit a real data access or deletion request, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Exercise your own real right to access, export or delete your data.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else how the right to ask for your data back actually works.

themes.theme: Faces, voices and biometrics
themes.description: What is different about data you cannot change — face, voice, fingerprint — and where it is being collected.
themes.transfer_check: Identify two places your biometrics are held, and for one of them find the policy on how it is stored and removed.

bands.K–2: Notice that your face unlocks a family tablet, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Explain why a fingerprint can't be changed like a password, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Explain what makes biometric data different from a password, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Decide, for a real service, whether to enable biometric login and why.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real risk of data you cannot change once it leaks.

themes.theme: A smaller footprint on purpose
themes.description: Aliases, minimal sign-ups and deleting the account you no longer use — shrinking the trail without leaving modern life.
themes.transfer_check: Close one dormant account fully and document the steps so someone else could follow them.

bands.K–2: Help an adult delete an old account you don't use anymore.
bands.3–5: Find one unused account to delete, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Delete a real unused account or minimise a real sign-up, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Reduce your own real digital footprint on purpose, deleting what you don't need.
bands.11–12: Help someone else audit and shrink their real digital footprint.

tracks.name: Working with AI: help, judgement and limits

themes.theme: What the machine is actually doing
themes.description: Pattern, prediction and training data — a working model of how an AI system produces an answer, without the mathematics.
themes.transfer_check: Explain to someone else, with one concrete example, why an AI system can be fluent and wrong at the same time.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult how a talking toy guesses what to say next.
bands.3–5: Explain that an AI guesses the next word from patterns, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Explain pattern and prediction in a real AI tool's output, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, using a real example, how training data shapes a real AI's answers.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else a working model of how a real AI tool actually works.

themes.theme: The question shapes the answer
themes.description: Context, constraints and examples: asking in a way that gets useful work instead of confident filler.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real task, ask an AI twice — once vaguely, once well — and present both answers with the differences marked.

bands.K–2: Ask a question two different ways and see the different answers, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Rewrite a question to get a better answer from a helper tool, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Rewrite a real prompt with context and examples to get a better answer, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Craft a real prompt with constraints and examples to get a reliably better answer.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to shape a real question to get a useful AI answer.

themes.theme: Checking the machine's work
themes.description: Verification habits for facts, citations, code and arithmetic that come out of a model.
themes.transfer_check: Find and document one real error in an AI answer, and show the check that caught it.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult to double-check something a helper tool said.
bands.3–5: Check one fact a helper tool gave you against a book or an adult.
bands.6–8: Verify a real AI-generated fact, citation or calculation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Verify real AI output — facts, code, citations — on your own before using it.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else a verification habit for real AI-generated work.

themes.theme: What not to paste into the box
themes.description: Secrets, other people's data and anything you could not stand to see again — what leaves your hands when you prompt.
themes.transfer_check: Write the do-not-paste list for your own life or workplace and apply it to three real prompts.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult before typing your name into a helper tool.
bands.3–5: Name one thing you should never type into a helper tool, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify what should never go into a real AI tool's prompt box, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Keep real secrets and others' data out of a real AI tool, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else what never belongs in an AI prompt and why.

themes.theme: Where AI already decides about you
themes.description: Feeds, prices, applications, moderation — the systems already scoring you, and which decisions you can appeal to a human.
themes.transfer_check: Identify two automated decisions that touched you this month and find the appeal or review path for one.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if a computer helped decide what ad you saw.
bands.3–5: Name one place a computer might already be deciding things for you, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real system — a feed, a price, an application — shaped by AI, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify, for a real decision affecting you, where AI already played a role.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real systems already using AI to decide about people.

themes.theme: Generated media and the shrinking proof
themes.description: Voices, faces and events that never happened — what deepfakes change about evidence, and the verification that still works.
themes.transfer_check: Given one suspect clip or image, run a provenance check and deliver a verdict with your reasoning.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult if a funny video of an animal talking is real.
bands.3–5: Spot one sign that a picture or video might be fake, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real generated image, voice or video, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Verify a real suspicious piece of media on your own before trusting it.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to spot and verify real generated media.

themes.theme: Doing your own work with the machine in the room
themes.description: The line between help and substitution in school and work, and how to use AI while still becoming good at the thing.
themes.transfer_check: For one real assignment or task, write the usage rule you followed and show what you did yourself and what the tool did.

bands.K–2: Draw your own picture even when a helper tool could draw one, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Write your own sentence first, then compare it to a helper tool's, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Use a real AI tool for help without letting it replace your own real work, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Draw the line, on your own real assignment, between help and substitution.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else where the line sits between AI help and doing the work yourself.

themes.theme: When the machine should not be alone
themes.description: Medical, legal, financial and safety calls: where AI output is a draft for a human, never the decision.
themes.transfer_check: Take one high-stakes question, get an AI answer, then show what a qualified human source added or corrected.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult before believing a helper tool's advice about being sick.
bands.3–5: Name one kind of decision a helper tool shouldn't make alone, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real medical, legal or safety decision that needs a human, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Recognise a real high-stakes decision where AI output alone is not enough.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why medical, legal or safety calls need a human in the loop.

themes.theme: The people inside the pipeline
themes.description: Data labellers, moderators, artists and authors — whose work trains a model and what fairness to them looks like.
themes.transfer_check: Trace one AI product to two kinds of human labour it depends on, with sources.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult who helps teach a helper tool what is right and wrong.
bands.3–5: Name one kind of worker who helps make AI tools work, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real worker's role — labeller, moderator, artist — behind a real AI tool, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Explain, for a real AI product, whose labour trained or moderated it.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the real people whose work is inside an AI pipeline.

themes.theme: Saying no to the tool
themes.description: Tasks where the honest answer is not to automate — and how to decline well when the pressure is to use it anyway.
themes.transfer_check: Name one real task you chose to do without AI, and defend the choice in a paragraph that convinces a sceptic.

bands.K–2: Choose to do a task by hand instead of asking a helper tool, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Pick one task you'll do yourself instead of using a helper tool, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real task better done without automation, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Choose, for a real task, to say no to the tool and explain why.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to recognise when the honest answer is not to automate.

tracks.name: Being online together: conduct, harm and repair

themes.theme: The person on the other end
themes.description: Why distance and screens loosen conduct, and the habits that keep a human in view when you type.
themes.transfer_check: Rewrite one real heated message — yours or a public one — so it could be said across a kitchen table.

bands.K–2: Say something kind to a friend online with an adult watching.
bands.3–5: Explain why a screen makes it easier to say something mean, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real message that forgot there was a person on the other end, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Catch yourself before sending a real message you wouldn't say in person.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else why distance online loosens conduct, using a real example.

themes.theme: Groups, chats and the rules nobody wrote
themes.description: Norms in group chats, servers and comment sections: reading them fast and knowing which ones you can change.
themes.transfer_check: Write down the actual rules of one group you belong to, and confirm them against what happens there in practice.

bands.K–2: Notice one rule a family group chat follows, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Name one unwritten rule of a group chat you're in, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Read the norms of a real group chat or server correctly, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read and follow the unwritten norms of a real group chat or server on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to a new member the unwritten rules of a real group you belong to.

themes.theme: Harassment: naming it early
themes.description: The line between disagreement, pile-on and campaign, and why targets are told it is smaller than it is.
themes.transfer_check: Given one real or case-study thread, mark where it crossed the line and say what the first responder should have done.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult if someone keeps saying mean things to you online.
bands.3–5: Explain the difference between one mean comment and many, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Identify a real pattern of pile-on or campaign behaviour, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Name a real harassment pattern early and act on it, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the line between disagreement, pile-on and campaign.

themes.theme: Blocking, muting, reporting
themes.description: The tools every platform hides in a different menu, what each one actually does, and when each is the right size.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate block, mute and report on a platform you use, and match each to a situation where it is the correct tool.

bands.K–2: Find the block button with an adult's help on a family device.
bands.3–5: Use a mute or block button on a practice account, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Correctly block, mute or report a real account, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Choose the right tool — block, mute or report — for a real situation, on your own.
bands.11–12: Show someone else where every platform hides these tools and when to use each.

themes.theme: Being the bystander who moves
themes.description: Documenting, checking on the target, refusing the amplification — what help looks like when the pile-on is happening.
themes.transfer_check: For one witnessed or case-study incident, carry out the bystander steps and record what you did and in what order.

bands.K–2: Tell an adult if you see someone being mean to a friend online.
bands.3–5: Check on a friend who got a mean comment, with an adult's help.
bands.6–8: Document and check on a real target of online harassment, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Act as a bystander who moves — documenting, checking, refusing to amplify — on a real case.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else what an effective bystander does when harm is happening online.

themes.theme: The mistake that is public forever
themes.description: Old posts, resurfaced jokes and the difference between accountability and permanent exile — for others and for your younger self.

bands.K–2: Ask an adult before posting something you might regret later.
bands.3–5: Think about whether a post could embarrass you later, with an adult.
bands.6–8: Find and reflect on an old post that no longer fits who you are, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Address a real old post of your own that resurfaced, on your own.
bands.11–12: Explain to someone else the difference between accountability and pile-on for old posts.

themes.theme: Arguing so it is worth it
themes.description: Steel-manning, asking one real question, and leaving a thread while it is still a conversation.

bands.9–10: Argue a real disagreement online worth having, on your own, and know when to leave it.
bands.11–12: Teach someone else how to steel-man an opponent's point before responding.

bands.6–8: Identify a real romance scam or fake marketplace listing, with a checker.
